ms: The amount by which sales/output (1)
exceed the break-even level of output (1)
Allow: actual sales − break-even sales (2)
questions.model: The margin of safety is the amount by which a business’s sales exceed its break-even level of output.
questions.tip: It can be shown in units or in revenue.

questions.q:
CityCabs is a taxi business with 15 cars.

Identify one fixed cost and one variable cost for CityCabs. [2]
ms: Fixed cost (1), e.g. insurance, vehicle licences, rent of office/garage, booking-app subscription, loan repayments/interest, salaries of office staff
Variable cost (1), e.g. fuel, tyres/maintenance linked to distance driven, drivers’ pay per trip/commission, cleaning per journey
questions.model:
Fixed cost: insurance for the cars.
Variable cost: fuel, because it rises with the number of journeys made.
questions.tip: A variable cost changes with output — for a taxi firm, output is journeys or kilometres. Marking: Do not accept ‘wages’ without qualification for either.

questions.q:
BrightLamps makes desk lamps. Fixed costs are $24 000 per month. Each lamp sells for $15 and has variable costs of $9.

(a) Calculate the break-even level of output. [2]
(b) Calculate the profit when BrightLamps sells 5 500 lamps in a month. [2]
ms: (a) M1: contribution per unit = 15 − 9 = $6, and 24 000 ÷ 6
(a) A1: 4 000 lamps
(b) A1: $9 000 (ecf from (a))
questions.tip: Check: margin of safety (1 500) × contribution ($6) = $9 000 — the same answer.

questions.q:
A break-even chart for a business is described below:
• The fixed cost line is horizontal at $10 000.
• The total revenue line starts at $0 and reaches $40 000 at an output of 2 000 units.
• The total cost line starts at $10 000 and reaches $30 000 at an output of 2 000 units.

Use this information to calculate:
(a) the selling price per unit [1]
(b) the variable cost per unit [1]
(c) the break-even level of output. [2]
ms: (c) A1: 1 000 units (ecf from (a) and (b))
questions.model:
(a) Price = $40 000 ÷ 2 000 = $20 per unit.
(b) Total variable cost at 2 000 units = $30 000 − $10 000 = $20 000, so variable cost = $20 000 ÷ 2 000 = $10 per unit.
(c) Contribution = $20 − $10 = $10. Break-even = $10 000 ÷ $10 = 1 000 units.
questions.tip: Total cost includes fixed cost — subtract the fixed cost before finding variable cost per unit.

questions.q:
GoBottle makes reusable water bottles. Each bottle sells for $18 and has variable costs of $10. Fixed costs are $30 000 per month. The factory currently produces and sells 4 000 bottles per month and has spare capacity.

A school chain offers to buy an extra 500 bottles per month at a special price of $12 each, with the school logo printed on them.

(a) Calculate GoBottle’s monthly profit now and its monthly profit if it accepts the order. [4]
(b) Should GoBottle accept the order? Justify your answer. [4]
ms: (a) A1: current profit = $2 000
(a) M1: extra profit from order = (12 − 10) × 500 = $1 000 (fixed costs unchanged)
(a) A1: new profit = $3 000 (ecf)
(b) Argument for accepting, e.g. positive contribution of $2 per bottle so profit rises from $2 000 to $3 000; uses spare capacity (1)
(b) Further point, e.g. new customer, possible repeat orders/publicity in schools (1)
(b) Argument against, e.g. logo printing adds cost (loss if over $2 per bottle); regular customers may demand lower prices; low profit per bottle (1)
(b) Justified decision with a condition, e.g. accept if printing costs are below $2 per bottle and the price is kept confidential (1)
questions.model:
(a) Contribution per bottle = $18 − $10 = $8. Current profit = $8 × 4 000 − $30 000 = $32 000 − $30 000 = $2 000.
The special order gives a contribution of $12 − $10 = $2 per bottle × 500 = $1 000. Fixed costs are already covered, so the new profit = $2 000 + $1 000 = $3 000.
(b) Accepting the order increases profit by 50%, from $2 000 to $3 000, and uses spare factory capacity that would otherwise be wasted. It could also lead to more orders from the school chain. However, printing the school logo may add costs; if it costs more than $2 per bottle the order would make a loss. Regular customers who pay $18 might also ask for lower prices if they hear about the $12 deal.
I think GoBottle should accept, because its current profit is very small and the order adds $1 000 a month without increasing fixed costs. It should first check that the logo printing costs less than $2 per bottle and agree that the special price stays confidential.
questions.tip: For a special order with spare capacity, fixed costs don’t change — only compare price with variable cost. Marking: max 2 marks in (b) without a decision.

questions.q:
BrightLamps has fixed costs of $24 000 per month, a selling price of $15 and variable costs of $9 per lamp. It sells 5 500 lamps a month, making a profit of $9 000. The marketing manager wants to raise the price to $18. She forecasts that monthly sales would fall to 4 200 lamps.

Should BrightLamps raise its price to $18? Justify your answer, using calculations to support your answer. [6]
ms: Indicative content — K/App (up to 2), An (up to 2), Ev (up to 2):
Calculation: new contribution = 18 − 9 = $9; new profit = 9 × 4 200 − 24 000 = 37 800 − 24 000 = $13 800 (up $4 800 from $9 000)
New break-even = 24 000 ÷ 9 = 2 667 lamps (2 666.7) — lower than 4 000; margin of safety 4 200 − 2 667 = 1 533 (about 1 533)
For: higher profit; lower break-even → less risky

Against: forecast may be wrong (demand may be more price-elastic); competitors may keep lower prices → market share falls; fewer customers may affect brand awareness/long-term sales; staff/capacity under-used

Ev: justified decision using the figures and recognising uncertainty, e.g. raise price because profit rises by $4 800 even with fewer sales, but only if the forecast is reliable / test the price first

levels.d: Accurate calculations used to analyse the effects on profit and break-even, with a justified decision that considers the reliability of the forecast or other factors.
Some correct calculation or developed analysis of effects of the price rise; decision weakly justified.
Knowledge of effects of price changes with little or no calculation.

questions.model:
At $18, contribution per lamp = $18 − $9 = $9. Profit = $9 × 4 200 − $24 000 = $37 800 − $24 000 = $13 800. This is $4 800 more than the current $9 000.
The new break-even output would be $24 000 ÷ $9 = 2 667 lamps (rounded up), much lower than the current 4 000, so the margin of safety is 1 533 lamps and the business is less likely to make a loss.
However, the 4 200 sales figure is only a forecast. If customers are more price-sensitive than expected and switch to cheaper competitors, sales could fall further. Lower sales may also reduce market share and brand awareness in the long term.
I recommend raising the price, because even if sales fell to about 3 600 lamps the profit would still be about $8 400, close to today’s level, so the risk is limited, while the forecast shows a 53% increase in profit. BrightLamps should test the new price for a short period and check what competitors charge before committing.
questions.tip: Calculate profit at BOTH prices — the decision should rest on the comparison.
